newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French staff demand halt to bank "giveaway".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French staff demand halt to bank "giveaway".

text.p: Staff and union leaders occupying the Paris headquarters of Credit Foncier said on Thursday they would press a mediator for solid guarantees that the government would halt a planned break-up that amounted to a "giveaway".

Seizing on remarks by government spokesman Alain Lamassoure that draft legislation concerning the break-up was being "kept in waiting", unions decided to push mediator Philippe Rouvillois for solid guarantees that the plan would be put on hold.

"We're looking for a strong signal from the state, at the moment it appears the (break-up) plan has been frozen," a trade union representative told Reuters, as the occupation by several hundred staff ground into its seventh day.

The government has been planning to allow cooperatively run Credit Immobilier to take over the home loans business of Credit Foncier and pass legislation to set up a state holding company which would take over and wind down the rest of the group.
"It's a free gift the government is offering," to Credit Immobilier," the union member said, asking not to be named.
"The French people rose up against giving part of Thomson to Daewoo for one symbolic franc. In our case it's not even for a symbolic franc, it's for nothing," the unionist said.

The government scrapped plans late last year to sell state electronics company Thomson SA to Lagardere after a veto from France's privatisation commission and an outcry by staff against the sale of Thomson's indebted TV and video subsidiary to South Korea's Daewoo Electronics for one symbolic franc.

"We want to see Credit Immobilier play the role of a real takeover partner, which means paying for what it takes, or else that it takes a stake in our capital like any other partner would do," the union member said.

Unions were preparing to meet government-appointed mediator Philippe Rouvillois at 1430 GMT after meeting his preconditions by releasing chairman Jerome Meyssonnier and seven board members on Wednesday.
"If there is a formula other than the one on the table at the moment, we are fully open to negotiation," Lamassoure said.

"In the meantime, and this is very important, the draft law which was prepared by the government to save the business ... and avoid all straight layoffs at Credit Foncier is being kept in waiting," he told RTL radio.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis unveiled plans in July for a partial takeover of the 145-year-old bank by Credit Immobilier and close the rest down in the coming years.

He says Credit Immobilier is the only solution on offer and would secure the jobs of 1,500 staff and that another 800 would be kept working for the new state holding company. Plans to offer the rest of the 3,300 staff early retirement packages had been in the pipeline before the break-up plan was announced in the summer.
Staff have been taking turns preparing food and spending the night in the giant, marble-columned central hall in sleeping bags, but also keeping bank branches open for business.
Meyssonnier said after his release talks he would push on with attempts to find the best solution for staff at the bank best known for providing cheap home loans to poorer families.
Amid record unemployment and intense media coverage, Arthuis has been under mounting pressure from opposition politicians and some from his own political camp to find another way out.
Credit Foncier has already been "nationalised" in the first stage of the break-up after losing 11 billion francs ($2 billion) in 1995, but expects a profit of one billion for 1996.
